extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, and practitioners of comedy (playwrights, humorists, literary theorists)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic guidance for producing comic effects in language, situation, and character — emphasising sentence-transformation (inversion, pun, transposition), gestures vs actions, and the social/psychological conditions that make characters laughable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Reverse elements of a sentence (e.g., put the subject in the object's place and vice versa) to obtain an unexpected meaning; a simple experimental device often used by professional wits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Labiche comedy exchange: 'What do you mean by emptying your pipe on to my terrace?' / 'What do you mean by putting your terrace under my pipe?' Notes: Inversion is 'the least interesting of the three' laws of comic sentence-transformation but easy to apply. Use to refute an idea humorously or to create a quick verbal flip. Anti-pattern: inversion that produces nonsense rather than a still-sensible reversed sentence will fail to amuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference (pun and play upon words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring two independent sets of ideas into the same expression so they 'interfere' with one another. This ranges from puns (homophonic different sentences masquerading as one) to true plays upon words where one sentence legitimately expresses two distinct ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pun (low form): same sound, different words/meanings — often disreputable. True play upon words: a single sentence legitimately yields two meanings, often by using figurative vs literal senses of a word. Effect: reveals a 'lapse of attention' in language and is amusing because language seems to forget its function. Anti-patterns: crude homophonic puns that feel merely lazy; if the dual meaning depends on different words (not one sentence), the effect is weaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition (comic transposition of expression into another key)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transpose the natural expression of an idea into a different 'key' or style (e.g., use a solemn style for trivial matter or a familiar style for the solemn) — the general rule: 'A COMIC EFFECT IS ALWAYS OBTAINABLE BY TRANSPOSING THE NATURE EXPRESSION OF AN IDEA INTO ANOTHER KEY.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the most far-reaching method for comic language, analogous to repetition in situation. You need not show both the natural and transposed expression; the audience supplies the missing natural one. Transposition can range from buffoonery to refined irony. Anti-pattern: transposition that is too subtle for the audience to supply the natural counterpart may fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody (transpose solemn into familiar)
rubrics_metrics.description: Express the solemn in familiar or modern terms (or otherwise degrade a dignified subject into the commonplace) to obtain a comic effect; an instance of transposition from solemn to trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Jean Paul Richter's dawn described 'like a lobster being boiled.' Also applies to treating ancient/classical matter in modern slang. Some theorists call this 'degradation.' Use when the contrast between register and topic is clear. Anti-pattern: parody that misunderstands or lacks a clear solemn referent will not read as parody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degradation / Transposition downward (familiarise the elevated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat something dignified as mean or trivial (a form of transposition that some define as 'degradation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produces comic effect by making the formerly dignified appear mean. Note: degradation is only one form of transposition; do not over-rely on it. Anti-pattern: overuse can become merely insulting rather than funny; subtlety often works better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration (treat small as large)
rubrics_metrics.description: Speak of small things as though they were large; systematic and prolonged exaggeration is comic and constitutes a form of transposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produces mock-heroic effects and sustained laughter when methodical. Example targets: braggadocio turned mock-heroic. Anti-pattern: single-off hyperbole may be merely absurd rather than comic unless sustained or patterned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition upward in moral value (treat the disreputable with utmost respectability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe scandalous, low-class, or disgraceful situations in the language of 'respectability' (formal, reputable language), creating comic contrast by moral transposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Dickens, Thackeray, Gogol. A single formal word can reveal 'an entire system of transposition' and make the situation comic. Particularly effective in exposing a 'moral organisation of immorality.' Anti-pattern: if the audience lacks the social register context, the irony may be lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony vs Humour (real vs ideal transposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish two transposition directions: stating what ought to be as if it is (IRONY — oratorical) versus describing what is with scrupulous minuteness and pretending it's what ought to be (HUMOUR — scientific).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irony is pitched towards an ideal and can become passionate eloquence; humour delights in technical detail and concrete facts, acting like a moralist disguised as a scientist. Use irony for rhetorical high-minded mockery; use humour for dispassionate, detailed depiction that exposes the comic. Anti-pattern: confusing the two tones will blunt effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional or business jargon transposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Transfer professional vocabulary or commercial phraseology into everyday social relations to comic effect (e.g., treating marriage as a business transaction in strictly commercial language).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Labiche ('Your kindness of the third ult.'), scenes where professions' technical terms are applied to domestic life. Can attain depth when it reveals character faults. Anti-pattern: jargon so obscure that readers cannot see the parallel will fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition ↔ Transposition analogy (language comedy parallels situational repetition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Language transposition plays the same role as repetition does in classic situation-comedy: transferring an idea into fresh surroundings or restaging it in a different register produces comic effects analogous to repeating a scene with variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of transposition as the language equivalent of repeating scenes between masters and servants etc. Use to create pattern and expectation the audience can complete. Anti-pattern: without an underlying familiar reference the transposition loses its punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsociability (lack of adaptability to society) as a source of comic character
rubrics_metrics.description: Any individual who automatically goes his own way without modelling himself on his social environment becomes comic; laughter functions as a social corrective to absentmindedness and unsociability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic characters are those who fail to adapt to society's implicit rules — their rigidity invites laughter. Example: Alceste (honest but unsociable) — seriousness or morality is less relevant than social flexibility. Anti-pattern: if the character's unsociability evokes pity or sympathy rather than distance, laughter will be impaired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigidity / Automatism / Absentmindedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigid, ready-made, automatic habits in a person (the mechanical element) make them laughable; the deeper the absentmindedness (systematic automatism), the higher the comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effect stems from involuntary gestures or unconscious remarks that betray a side of the person they do not perceive. Examples: Don Quixote's systematic absentmindedness; characters contradicting their own prescriptions. Anti-pattern: if the person appears self-aware about the trait, the automatism/rigidity loses comic force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation of feeling (parasitic emotion) preventing sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a serious vice or feeling comic, the poet isolates it within the character so it remains parasitic and does not infect other mental states — this prevents the audience's sympathy from arising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: depict feelings as rigid, puppet-like, or disconnected from the whole personality so they fail to become contagious. Example: Harpagon's greed passes by other feelings 'absentmindedly.' Anti-pattern: if the feeling is portrayed as integrative and consuming, it will arouse sympathy and become tragic rather than comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on gestures not actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy directs attention to gestures — attitudes, movements, language that express mental states automatically — rather than to deliberate actions (which belong to drama).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gesture is automatic, explosive, and isolates part of the person; action is intentional and engages the whole person. Example: Tartuffe's gestures and utterances (locking hair-shirt) make him comic; his sincere material devotion to hypocrisy creates gestures that expose him. To create comedy, emphasize mannerisms, automatic phrases, and isolated movements. Anti-pattern: concentrating on large-scale intentional actions will push the piece toward drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must not arouse the spectator's emotions (indifference condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: For something serious or vicious to become comic it must not arouse sympathy, fear, or pity in the audience; absence of emotion in the spectator is the single necessary condition for laughter (though not sufficient).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the depiction of a fault or vice provokes authentic feeling, laughter is barred. The comic poet must lull sensibility or throw a 'wet blanket' on sympathy via techniques like isolation, emphasis on gesture, parody, or transposition. Anti-pattern: emotional engagement will transform the material into tragedy/drama rather than comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy aims at the general — types and stock characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy depicts general types (stock characters) rather than unique individuality; the ready-made, stereotyped elements of personality are what comedy crystallises and ridicules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because words denote genera and life simplifies for utility, comedy works by naming and exposing types. A comic character is often a type that others can fall into. Use generalized traits and reproducible mannerisms to craft comic types. Anti-pattern: overemphasising unique individuality and inner life moves the work away from comedic generality toward high art/drama.
